doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Dorsey band and moving to New York
title: Subbing around New York and its musical circles
summary: Subbing on varied jobs, a jazz wedding with Buddy Tate, and connected New York scenes like Greg Cohen and Zorn.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. And then I wound up having to move out of that apartment. That’s a whole other story, well we don’t have to get into that story, but so anyway, so six months nothing. No work. I was ready to take a day job. I’d never worked, in fact I never have — knock on wood — never have done anything but music my whole life, since I was ten. So this was really depressing for me. And I actually talked my way into a job with a photo, one of these photo processing labs, Gene Berry Photos, as the Assistant Manager. And I knew nothing about photos, nothing about being an Assistant Manager. So I was ready to show up for work on Monday morning. I got up, I just thought about this. I called the guy and said “I know you’re not going to understand this, but I can’t do this job.” And I just hung in there for another few weeks. I started getting calls to sub on other bands. This is what happens in New York. You have to stay there long enough to get your name around, and you have to do as many circles of jobs as you can before you find what it is that you want to do. So you wind up subbing for a lot of musicians, big bands, Latin bands, weddings, anything. In fact I remember playing a wedding pretty soon after I moved to New York with Buddy Tate on saxophone, Mel Lewis on drums and Steve Kuhn on piano.
Yes. And I thought to myself, geez, either the weddings here are really great or the musicians are scuffling a little more than I would like. And it’s kind of in between the two.
Yeah. I mean those guys, that particular gig, were they playing the standard wedding stuff?

No. See in New York there are more jazz-oriented weddings. Like people will hire a jazz band in New York like they would hire a string quartet because they want to have some class for an evening. Although there’s countless numbers of stories where you go in telling these people, this is all we do, this is what we play, and then you get there and they want to hear —
They want to hear “Celebration.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Yeah. That’s the tune all right. And “New York New York” you know and stuff like that. But I think on that job they left them alone though. That was a kind of a nice job. But I couldn’t believe that. It’s really surprising around New York, the people you run into in the most unexpected places. But that’s the beauty of it too because you keep meeting new faces and new musical circles. There’s all these little groups around New York that do different things. And one guy plays not only in this group of people but in this group, so there’s the connection. So in fact the bass player I have in my band now, Greg Cohen, plays with John Zorn’s band also. I don’t know if you’re —

So I’ve been talking a lot to some of those guys. In fact I’m talking to this clarinet player Marty Ehrlich about doing some recording together and trying to find a common bond. I love doing that. It’s a challenge for me because I like their music a lot and it’s good sometimes to test myself and see what I can bring to that kind of music. So anyway, when I first moved to New York that also was a huge big experience for me. And there’s a few highlights like that I could talk about. Working with Benny Goodman, of course playing the clarinet, he was a big idol for me.
